newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean strikes run out of steam.
newsitem.headline: South Korean strikes run out of steam.

text.p: Militant South Korean workers resumed industrial action after the New Year's break on Friday, but strikes that crippled industry late last year seemed to be running out of steam.
An outlawed union body threatened to escalate unrest next week unless the government revoked a controversial labour law.
However, Friday's strike call by the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions to workers at car plants and selected industrial facilities received only a mixed response.
The 500,000-member confederation claimed 46 unions and 96,158 workers answered its call. The Labour Ministry's more modest estimate was 31 unions and 22,884 workers.
Union leader Kwon Young-kil accused the government of scaling down the numbers and plotting to "paint the confederation as backing down".

He told a news conference if the government did not revoke the labour law the confederation would escalate its action to embrace workers from the giant Hyundai Group as well as construction and office workers on Monday.
On Tuesday it would bring out public sector unions covering hospitals, subways and broadcasters.
"If the government does not meet our demands we are ready to order a national strike, carry out street demonstrations and wage an all-out battle," he said.

A wave of strikes crippled industry last week when the ruling party, in a clandestine session of parliament, rammed through a labour law allowing companies to replace strikers, hire temporary staff and lay off workers.
The work stoppages, which hit car and ship production, hospitals and subways, were postponed until after the New Year holidays to spare the public chaos.
The more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the largest umbrella group with 1.3 million members postponed its strikes until after January 11.
"We are being cautious with our decision to order a strike," said federation official Kim Sung-jin.
The federation ordered subway train drivers to hold off a 48-hour strike scheduled for Saturday.

The union at Kia Motors said 18,000 workers went back on strike on Friday and would continue until the law was reversed. But the company's public relations office said Friday was a holiday and workers were not expected back until Monday.
Daewoo Motor Co was on a partial strike on Friday afternoon, and its union said it would hold a two-hour strike on Saturday morning. Plans for Monday were still undecided.
Hyundai Heavy Industries' union said 7,000 of 27,500 employees took legal leave on Friday in a protest gesture.
Halla Heavy Industries' union said 90 percent of its workers walked out today. The company declined comment.
The union umbrella bodies plan a string of rallies over the weekend, and citizen groups are continuing their protests.
"I feel it is wrong the way the laws were passed," said Kang Sung-hwan, a local businessman after signing a protest petition organised by a citzen's group.
"Our businesses need to suffer a bit for this country to grow up," Kang said in support of the strikes.

Kim Jun-il, a researcher at the Korea Development Institute, the government's leading economic think-tank, said changes in the law would benefit both unions and employers by creating a more flexible labour market.
